take: Crude’s push toward $100 on the expanding Middle East conflict and the shutdown of Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline is the dominant story, with the Houthis now occupying Mokha and Perim Island and sitting astride Bab el-Mandeb, whilst Hormuz transits collapsed to single digits over the weekend and a container ship was struck off Qeshm with one seafarer killed; that combination of a severed Saudi bypass route and a chokepoint under fire is precisely what keeps the geopolitical premium bid and drags central banks back onto inflation alert. The freight transmission is already visible — Singapore still sold a record 37.77 million mt of bunkers in January–August despite the Hormuz crisis, owners report no difficulty sourcing bunkers, and Aegean has cashed in a 2022-built aframax/LR2 for around $83m, all of which tells you the rerouting is lengthening tonne-miles rather than destroying demand. On the positioning side, the EIA has the US averaging a record 13.8 million b/d in 2026 against 13.7 million b/d in 2025, elevated crack spreads are pulling pump prices higher, and US LNG exports ran at 17.4 Bcf/d in H1, up 23% year on year, so the barrels and molecules are there — the squeeze is logistical, not geological. The cross-market link to watch is the gasoil-versus-bunker spread: with Singapore volumes at record pace and product exports from Nigeria up seven-fold since 2023 on the back of Dangote, the marginal barrel is increasingly Atlantic-basin and eastbound, which keeps VLSFO and gasoil cracks tethered to the same Middle East risk premium. In the next 24 hours, watch Hormuz transit counts and any further UKMTO advisories, the Saudi pipeline restart headlines, and whether Brent holds the $100 handle into the US session — that is the line that decides whether central banks merely jawbone or actually move.
